title: Freedom of conscience
hook: a thread the Gurus did not wear, and the ninth Guru gave his life for others' right to wear it

segments.voice: Yesterday, detachment in the home: fragrance in a flower, a face in a mirror. Your line was home, held lightly. What did you let go of, and whom did you hold? Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

A cotton thread, worn across the chest. For some Hindu families it's the janeu, the sacred thread, put on in a ceremony and worn for life. In a passage of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak declines that thread. He asks instead for a thread spun from compassion and contentment, one that never breaks or burns. So Guru Nanak set it aside. And yet the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, is remembered for giving his life so that other people could keep wearing theirs. Today is about how those two things fit together.
screen: `A COTTON THREAD ACROSS THE CHEST.` → `GURU NANAK DECLINES IT.` → `THE NINTH GURU DIES FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as Sikh tradition tells it. A group of Kashmiri Pandits, Hindu scholars, came to Guru Tegh Bahadur at Anandpur. The Mughal authorities were pressing them to give up their faith and convert. Tradition says the Guru's young son, the future tenth Guru, was there, and said that such a moment needed someone great to stand up. The Guru told the Pandits to send word to the emperor: if he converts, we will too. Then he went to Delhi. He was arrested and, refusing to give up his faith, he was executed in the city, at a spot Sikhs now mark with Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib. Later, a work attributed to the tenth Guru, the Bachittar Natak, sums it up, paraphrased: he protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread; he gave his head, but not his resolve. Hold that next to Guru Nanak's hymn. Guru Nanak had set the thread aside. His path had its own way. And the ninth Guru died for the right of people to keep a way that wasn't his. That is freedom of conscience, made concrete. Not my faith, my right. Their faith, their right. One more thing matters here. The pressure in the story came from the power of a state, not from the faith of ordinary neighbors. In Sikh memory, this is a stand against force, not against any people or any religion. The Guru's answer wasn't to force anyone back. It was to stand between the weak and the strong, and not move.
screen: `THE PANDITS COME TO ANANDPUR.` · `THE GURU GOES TO DELHI.` · `HE GAVE HIS HEAD, NOT HIS RESOLVE.` · `A WAY THAT WASN'T HIS.` · then, large: `THEIR FAITH, THEIR RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: defend someone's freedom. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose way of believing, praying or living is different from yours. A coworker who fasts. A neighbor who wears something you don't. A relative who left the tradition, or joined one. Hold them in mind with respect. Then think: where might their freedom be squeezed, even a little? A joke at their expense. A schedule that ignores their holy day. Find one small thing you could do to make room for them. If you pray, you can remember Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Freedom of conscience. The ninth Guru gave his life for the right of others to keep a faith that wasn't his own. Today's word.
Your line: their faith, their right. Today, do the one thing you found to make room for someone's different way, and do it without asking them to explain it. Day one thousand two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom with kirtan, readings of his hymns and gatherings at gurdwaras, including Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi, and speak of him as a defender of the freedom of faith.
